title: Designing a Plugin Interface
summary: A plugin is native code built separately from the game, possibly with a different compiler version, that the game loads at run time. The interface between them must therefore be a stable **C interface**: plain types, function pointers, explicit versions and sizes. This lesson designs Delve's plugin API in both directions (the **host API** the game offers plugins, and the **plugin API** plugins offer the game) using lessons 4.05, 3.04 and 12.06.
markdown:
## Two directions ```mermaid flowchart LR G["Delve (host)"] -->|"HostApi: functions plugins may call
log, spawn, give item, subscribe to events"| P["plugin.dll"] P -->|"PluginApi: functions the game calls
init, update, shutdown"| G ``` - The **host API** is what the game lets plugins do. It defines the plugin's powers, so it is designed carefully and kept small. - The **plugin API** is what every plugin must provide, so the game can initialise it, call it each frame, and shut it down. ## Rule 1: a C interface, not C++ classes The game and a plugin may be built with different compilers, settings or standard library versions. Lesson 4.05 explained why `std::string`, `std::vector` and C++ classes with virtual functions must not cross that boundary. The interface uses only: - integers, floats, and fixed-size plain structs; - `const char*` strings in UTF-8, valid only for the duration of the call (copy them if you need them later); - function pointers; - opaque handles (`typedef struct DelveEntity* DelveEntityHandle;`, or plain integer ids, lesson 3.10). ## Rule 2: tables of function pointers, with a version and a size Both directions are **structs of function pointers**, the hand-made vtables of lesson 3.05's practice task, each starting with lesson 12.06's version and size: ```cpp-norun // delve_plugin.h: the only header plugins include. C-compatible. #pragma once #include #define DELVE_API_VERSION_MAJOR 1 #define DELVE_API_VERSION_MINOR 0 typedef struct DelveHostApi { uint32_t size; // sizeof(DelveHostApi) as the game was built: fields past it do not exist uint16_t versionMajor, versionMinor; void (*log)(const char* message); int (*spawnMonster)(const char* kind, int x, int y); // returns an entity id, or -1 int (*giveItem)(const char* itemId, int count); // returns how many did not fit int (*playerHealth)(void); void (*subscribe)(const char* eventName, void (*handler)(const char* eventName, int64_t value, void* user), void* user); // version 1.1 and later add fields here, at the end only } DelveHostApi; typedef struct DelvePluginApi { uint32_t size; uint16_t versionMajor, versionMinor; const char* name; int (*init)(const DelveHostApi* host); // return 0 for success void (*update)(double dt); // may be null if the plugin needs no per-frame work void (*shutdown)(void); } DelvePluginApi; // The one function every plugin DLL exports: // extern "C" __declspec(dllexport) int delvePluginEntry(DelvePluginApi* out); // The game passes a zeroed struct whose size it sets; the plugin fills it in. ``` Why this shape: - **One exported function** (`delvePluginEntry`) instead of many keeps `GetProcAddress` lookups to one and the export table simple (lesson 4.05). - **Function pointers in a struct** let the game add functions later (at the end, lesson 12.06) without breaking old plugins. - **`size` and the version** let each side check what the other supports: a plugin built for API 1.0 runs on a 1.3 game; a plugin needing 1.3 refuses politely on a 1.0 game. - **`void* user`** in callbacks lets a plugin get back its own state when the game calls it, since C function pointers carry no data (lesson 3.04). ## Rule 3: ownership is explicit Every pointer crossing the boundary has a documented owner and lifetime: - Strings passed **into** a plugin call are valid only during the call. - The host API table stays valid until `shutdown` returns. - Memory a plugin allocates, the plugin frees; memory the game allocates, the game frees (lesson 4.05: different heaps). Write these rules in comments in the header: it is the plugin authors' only documentation. ## Rule 4: the host API decides what plugins can do Every function in `DelveHostApi` is a capability given to code you did not write. Expose gameplay-level operations (spawn, give, read health, subscribe to events), validated like console commands (lesson 11.07), not raw pointers into the game's internals. A plugin that can only call `spawnMonster("goblin", x, y)` cannot corrupt the entity storage; one handed a pointer to it can. Native code can still do anything in principle (it runs in your process), but a good API means well-behaved plugins never need to. ## Common mistakes > [!warning] C++ types in the interface > `std::string`, `std::vector`, exceptions and classes do not cross a DLL boundary safely. Use C types. > [!warning] No version or size > The first change to the API breaks every existing plugin silently. > [!warning] Exposing internal pointers > Give plugins operations, not access to your data structures. > [!warning] Throwing exceptions across the boundary > C++ exceptions must not escape a plugin into the game (or the reverse). Catch them at the boundary and return error codes. ## Knowledge check ```quiz ? Why is the plugin interface written in C rather than C++ classes? + The game and plugins may be built with different compilers or settings, and only plain C types and function pointers are reliably compatible - C is faster - DLLs cannot contain C++ > Lesson 4.05's rules for DLL boundaries. ? Why does every API table start with a size and version? + So each side can tell which functions the other provides, and add new ones at the end without breaking old plugins - To make the struct aligned - Windows requires it > Lesson 12.06's versioning, applied to function tables. ? What is the `void* user` parameter in the event callback for? + It lets the plugin pass its own state pointer, which the game hands back when it calls the callback - It holds the event's value - It is reserved for the game > C function pointers carry no data; this pointer does. ```
ideas:
- Write `delve_plugin.h` and a game-side function that fills a `DelveHostApi`.
- Add a function to the host API in a version 1.1 and check a 1.0 plugin still works.
- Write the comment block documenting every pointer's lifetime.

cards.q: What are the host API and the plugin API?
cards.a: The host API is the table of functions the game offers plugins; the plugin API is the table of functions every plugin provides so the game can initialise, update and shut it down.

cards.q: What may cross the plugin boundary?
cards.a: Integers, floats, plain fixed-size structs, UTF-8 `const char*` strings valid for the call, function pointers and opaque handles or ids.

cards.q: How should errors cross the boundary?
cards.a: As return codes; C++ exceptions must be caught on their own side and never propagate across.
